## Biologists have a data problem. I build the tools.


```{=html}
<style>
/* Scoped to this deck. custom.scss is NOT modified, the shipping deck depends
   on it unchanged.

   v1 was code-first: the last line of a .walls card was always an identifier
   ("→ plotomics") and the label of a .flow box was always a function name
   (`set_selection`), so both are set in monospace blue. v2 is prose-first, those same slots now hold sentences, and monospace makes a sentence read as
   code. So: keep the colour and weight that mark them as labels, drop the
   typewriter face. */
.reveal .walls > div > p:last-child {
  font-family: inherit;
  font-size: .88em;
  color: #404041;
  opacity: .82;
}
.reveal .flow > div > p:first-child {
  font-family: inherit;
  font-size: 1em;
}

/* custom.scss ships a 3-column default and .c4; this deck also needs 2-up, and
   5-up for the ten apps. Ten cards over four columns leaves a 4-4-2 last row
   that reads as something missing; two rows of five reads as the count. */
.reveal .cards.c2 { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); }
.reveal .cards.c5 { grid-template-columns: repeat(5, 1fr); }

/* The five packages as their own stickers. Five across a 1280px slide leaves
   about 230px each, which holds the hex with room either side, and lets the
   one-line job wrap to two lines underneath without touching its neighbour. The
   name sits between them so the eye goes sticker, name, job, in that order.

   Sized by HEIGHT, not width. The five stickers are not all the same aspect
   ratio, and a shared width leaves the squarer ones visibly shorter than their
   neighbours, which reads as a mistake rather than as artwork. */
.reveal .hexrow {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(5, 1fr);
  gap: 1.1em;
  margin-top: .9em;
}
.reveal .hexrow > div { text-align: center; }
.reveal .hexrow img {
  display: block;
  height: 185px;
  width: auto;
  margin: 0 auto .5em;
}
.reveal .hexrow b {
  display: block;
  font-size: .62em;
  font-weight: 600;
  margin-bottom: .2em;
}
/* The ten apps, each as the card drawn for it. Five across leaves ~230px, and
   the art is 3:2, so a card is about 150px tall and two rows clear the slide
   with room for the name and its line. The image carries the recognition, the
   text carries the meaning, so neither has to do both. */
.reveal .appgrid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(5, 1fr);
  gap: .5em .75em;
  margin-top: .7em;
}
.reveal .appgrid > div {
  text-align: center;
  padding: .3em .3em .4em;
  border-radius: 4px;
}
/* Same job as .cards .on: mark the four the talk stops on, readable from the
   back, without a border that would fight the artwork's own frame. */
.reveal .appgrid > div.on { background: rgba(68, 112, 153, .11); }
.reveal .appgrid img {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
  margin: 0 auto .32em;
  border: 1px solid rgba(64, 64, 65, .16);
  border-radius: 3px;
}
.reveal .appgrid b {
  display: block;
  font-size: .52em;
  font-weight: 600;
  margin-bottom: .1em;
}
.reveal .appgrid span {
  display: block;
  font-size: .38em;
  line-height: 1.3;
  color: rgba(64, 64, 65, .85);
}

.reveal .hexrow span {
  display: block;
  font-size: .44em;
  line-height: 1.32;
  color: rgba(64, 64, 65, .85);
}

/* .on marks the cards the talk actually opens. The other six are names the
   room hears once and never sees again, so the mark has to survive a glance
   from the back of a Zoom grid: a tint plus a heavier left rule, not a colour
   swap that reads as decoration. The rest keep their white background and full
   contrast rather than being dimmed, because showing the range is the slide's
   other job and a greyed-out card looks disabled, not deprioritised. */
.reveal .cards > div.on {
  background: rgba(68, 112, 153, .09);
  border-left: 6px solid #447099;
}
.reveal .cards > div:not(.on) { border-left-color: rgba(64, 64, 65, .22); }

/* .push starts a right-hand group in a pill row. .pills is already a flex
   container, so margin-left:auto eats the free space and everything from here
   on sits against the right edge. This only works because the deck writes pills
   as raw HTML: through a fenced div Quarto wraps the spans in a <p>, that <p>
   becomes the flex item, and the push would stop at its shrink-wrapped width
   rather than the slide's. */
.reveal .pills span.push { margin-left: auto; }

/* custom.scss sets the bignum at 1.7em, sized for a slide where the numbers ARE
   the content. On the biobouncer slide they introduce a diagram that is the
   real argument, so they give their height back to it. */
.reveal .bignums { margin: .1em 0 .35em; }
.reveal .bignums > div > p:first-child { font-size: 1.3em; }
.reveal .bignums > div > p:last-child { font-size: .46em; }

/* .bbrow, the biobouncer stats band: two numbers and three pills on ONE row.
   Dropping the third bignum left the numbers occupying about 250px of a 1280px
   slide with the pills stacked underneath on their own line. Side by side they
   cost one band instead of two, and the ~75px that buys goes to the diagram,
   which is the actual argument of the slide. */
.reveal .bbrow {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 2.2em;
  margin: .1em 0 .3em;
}
.reveal .bbrow .bignums { margin: 0; flex: none; }
.reveal .bbrow .pills { margin: 0; }

/* .titlelogo, an app's own mark set INSIDE its h2 rather than parked in a
   corner. When the slide is titled with the app's name, the mark belongs next
   to the name; the old .applogo sat bottom-right and read as a watermark.
   Sized in em so it tracks the h2 and needs no retuning if the title changes.
   vertical-align optically centres a square mark against a cap-height word,
   which baseline alignment does not; it is tuned to the height below, so the
   two move together.

   Set taller than the cap height on purpose. At .92em the hex read as a bullet
   point next to the word rather than as the project's mark. */
.reveal h2 .titlelogo {
  display: inline-block;
  height: 1.34em;
  width: auto;
  margin: 0 .3em 0 0;
  vertical-align: -.32em;
  border: none;
  box-shadow: none;
}
/* Quarto wraps a lone image in a figure; inside an h2 that would break the
   line. Force it back to inline flow. */
.reveal h2 .quarto-figure,
.reveal h2 figure,
.reveal h2 p { display: inline; margin: 0; }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   .app, the name of the application on screen.

   Five consecutive slides each show a different app, and the name was buried
   as the first two words of a grey kicker sentence, in the same weight as the
   rest of it. From the back of a Zoom call there was nothing to tell you which
   app you were looking at. A chip pulls the name out of the sentence without
   needing a second line for it.
   --------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
.reveal .kicker .app {
  display: inline-block;
  margin-right: .45em;
  padding: .06em .5em .1em;
  border-radius: 3px;
  background: #447099;
  color: #FFFFFF;
  font-weight: 600;
  letter-spacing: .01em;
  /* The kicker is set in a lighter grey at reduced size; the chip has to sit
     ON that baseline, so it inherits the size rather than setting its own. */
  font-size: inherit;
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   Deck-wide vertical rhythm, tightened. A Playwright sweep of all 17 slides at
   1280x720 found the .payoff line hanging off the bottom of the canvas on SIX
   of them, by 3px on the mildest and 97px on the worst, which means it had been
   presenting sliced through its glyphs or missing entirely. Nothing about it is
   a regression; it is how the deck was built.

   The cause is not auto-stretch. Every figure here already carries .nostretch
   and an explicit width=, so the heights are a consequence of those width
   percentages, and the percentages were picked without checking what height
   they implied once an h2, a kicker and a payoff were also on the slide.

   Rather than shrink six figures, take it out of the rhythm: the affected
   slides carry 76-90px of inter-block whitespace and are over by 3-33px. These
   two lines buy about 41px on EVERY slide, which cannot break a slide that
   already fit, since the only effect is to give it more room. Slide 14 is the
   one that this does not rescue on its own; see the width= on its screenshot.
   --------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
.reveal .kicker { margin-bottom: .4em; }
.reveal .payoff { margin-top: .25em; padding-top: .28em; }
/* The 40px under every screenshot is the figure's OWN bottom margin, not the
   payoff's top margin, which is why tightening .payoff alone moved these slides
   by 18px instead of the projected 41. Measure before assuming which box owns
   a gap. */
.reveal .quarto-figure { margin-bottom: 0; }

/* This slide's vertical budget, measured in Chrome at 1280x720. It used to be
   over: h2 (91) + kicker (41) + five thumbnail rows (434) + pills (41) +
   payoff (70) plus the gaps came to 769px on a 720px canvas, so the payoff was
   rendering 49px below the bottom edge, sliced through its glyphs.

   The payoff is now gone, folded into the two right-hand pills, which returns
   about 90px. That goes straight back into the tiles, since the thumbnails are
   the entire argument of the slide. */
.reveal .viz26 { margin: .1em 0 0; }
.reveal .viz26 ~ .pills { margin: .25em 0 0; }
.reveal .viz26 .vrow {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;   /* label rail, then the tiles */
  align-items: center;
  gap: .6em;
  margin-bottom: .14em;
}
.reveal .viz26 .vlabel {
  display: flex;
  align-items: baseline;
  justify-content: space-between;
  gap: .5em;
  font-size: .46em;
  font-weight: 600;
  color: #404041;
  padding-right: .4em;
  border-right: 2px solid rgba(68, 112, 153, .3);
}
.reveal .viz26 .vlabel b { font-size: 1.5em; color: #447099; }
/* Always six columns, even on the four-tile rows. A row that stretched four
   tiles across the full width would make those categories look bigger than the
   six-tile ones, which is the opposite of what the counts are saying. */
.reveal .viz26 .vtiles {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(6, 1fr);
  gap: 5px;
}
.reveal .viz26 .vtiles img {
  width: 100%;
  display: block;
  margin: 0;
  border: 1px solid rgba(64, 64, 65, .22);
  border-radius: 2px;
  box-shadow: none;
  /* Taller than the source. The thumbs are natively 2.17:1; the payoff line
     leaving this slide freed about 90px, and spending it on height is what
     makes a 167px-wide tile actually readable from the back of a call. The
     cost is a slight top-and-bottom crop, which object-fit: cover below takes
     off both edges evenly. Set from the measured row height, not guessed. */
  aspect-ratio: 1.78 / 1;
  object-fit: cover;
}

/* .recipe, the two one-line captions bracketing the exported snippet on
   "You planned it before you paid for it". Small and grey so the code stays
   the thing being looked at. */
.reveal .recipe {
  font-size: .5em;
  color: #404041;
  opacity: .72;
  margin: .5em 0 .25em;
}
.reveal .recipe.after { margin: .25em 0 0; }
/* The default code block on this theme is sized for a slide with nothing else
   on it. Here it shares with a four-box flow row and two captions. */
.reveal .recipe + pre,
.reveal .recipe + div.sourceCode pre {
  font-size: .52em;
  line-height: 1.35;
  margin: 0;
}

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   .dna, what a variant actually is, for people who have never seen one.
   Two sequences, identical except for one letter. Drawn in CSS rather than
   shipped as an image: it stays sharp at any projector or Zoom resolution, it
   costs no bytes, and there is no licence attached to it.
   Base colours are the standard nucleotide scheme, so the one bioinformatician
   in the room reads it as correct rather than as decoration.
   --------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
.reveal .dna { margin: .35em 0 .2em; }
.reveal .dna .seq {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: .7em;
  margin-bottom: .3em;
}
.reveal .dna .who {
  flex: none;
  width: 6.4em;          /* wide enough that "this patient" stays on one line */
  text-align: right;
  font-size: .5em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  letter-spacing: .1em;
  opacity: .65;
}
.reveal .dna .strand {
  font-family: "Source Code Pro", Consolas, monospace;
  font-size: .82em;
  letter-spacing: .28em;
  font-weight: 600;
}
.reveal .dna .strand .A { color: #4C8C2B; }
.reveal .dna .strand .C { color: #1F6F8B; }
.reveal .dna .strand .G { color: #E8A33D; }
.reveal .dna .strand .T { color: #C1342E; }
.reveal .dna .hit {
  background: rgba(238, 99, 49, .16);
  outline: 2px solid #EE6331;
  border-radius: 2px;
  padding: 0 .1em;
}
/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   .vrsplit, the app two-up: explainer left, running app right. Used by both
   variant-reviewer and GeneScout.

   The video gets the larger track because it is the evidence; the left column
   is a fixed explainer that only has to stay readable. minmax(0, …) on BOTH
   tracks is copied from .withmeme in custom.scss and is load-bearing: a plain
   fr lets a wide child blow its track out and push the other column off the
   slide.

   The caption used to be .dna .cap, a block UNDER the strands carrying a 9.6em
   left margin to fake alignment with them. It now sits above them in its own
   column, so that hack is gone with it.
   --------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
.reveal .vrsplit {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 350px) minmax(0, 1fr);
  gap: 1.1em;
  align-items: center;
  margin-top: .35em;
}
.reveal .vrsplit .vrcap {
  font-size: .62em;
  line-height: 1.35;
  color: #404041;
  margin: 0 0 .55em;
}
/* The genome size in digits, not words. "Three billion" reads as a turn of
   phrase; the row of zeros reads as a measurement, which is the point of the
   sentence. Monospace so the zeros are even and survive Zoom's compression. */
.reveal .vrsplit .vrnum {
  font-family: "Source Code Pro", Consolas, monospace;
  font-weight: 600;
  white-space: nowrap;
}
.reveal .vrsplit .vrline {
  font-size: .58em;
  line-height: 1.35;
  color: #404041;
  opacity: .8;
  margin: .7em 0 0;
}
/* The clip drives its own height here rather than taking .vrvid's fixed 296px,
   because in this layout it is the column that should grow. */
.reveal .vrsplit .vrwrap { display: block; }
.reveal .vrsplit .demovid.vrvid { height: auto; width: 100%; }
.reveal .vrsplit .pills { margin: .1em 0 0; }

/* ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   .demovid, the seven screen recordings.

   NOT autoplay. reveal's data-autoplay starts a clip the instant the slide
   arrives, which takes the timing away from you: land early and the demo is
   already running while you are still talking, land late and you have missed
   the opening. These start on a click and toggle on every click after, so the
   clip runs when you say it does.

   Arrow keys are left alone deliberately. Space and the arrows still advance
   the deck, so there is no key that means "play here" and no way to trigger a
   clip by accident while navigating.

   data-src is reveal's lazy-load attribute. Note it does NOT keep the file out
   of the HTML: embed-resources base64s it anyway, so the deck carries all seven
   clips inline and remains one portable file at 71 MB. That was measured, not
   assumed: cold load in Chrome is 0.36 s. If a future clip does make load
   sluggish, the escape hatch is an attribute Quarto does not recognise,
   data-vsrc say, plus three lines of JS to copy it onto .src on slide change.
   --------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
/* Sized by HEIGHT with the aspect ratio pinned, not by width. Every clip is
   1920x1080 and the canvas is 1280x720, so driving off height fills the slide
   and still scales DOWN rather than up.

   aspect-ratio is what makes the border correct. Setting width:100% instead
   gave a 1218x622 box holding a 1105x622 picture, so the frame sat 56px off the
   content on each side, letterboxed against the element's own white.

   The bare .demovid is only ever the two untitled hero slides, DEMO and
   GALLERY, because .appvid and .vrvid below both override the height. Those two
   go FULL BLEED: a .heroslide section is a zero-padding 1280x720 box, and 16:9
   at 720 tall is exactly 1280 wide, so the clip is the slide. No border, since
   a frame on a full-bleed video is just a line the projector clips.

   The two things in the corners survive it. .act keeps its white pad and its
   z-index:2 further down, so GALLERY and DEMO stay readable on top of the
   video; the slide number and progress bar are reveal's own chrome and paint
   above it too. */
.reveal .demovid {
  display: block;
  margin: 0 auto;
  height: 720px;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  max-width: 100%;
  background: #FFFFFF;
  cursor: pointer;
}
/* The four app clips and the variant-reviewer clip share a slide with other
   content, so they keep the frame that separates them from the white. */
.reveal .demovid.appvid,
.reveal .demovid.vrvid { border: 1px solid rgba(64, 64, 65, .22); }
/* The DEMO and GALLERY slides have no title, so their clip takes the full
   frame. The variant-reviewer slide shares with a title, a kicker, the sequence
   graphic and a payoff line, so its clip gets what is left. */
.reveal .demovid.vrvid { height: 296px; }
/* The four app clips share their slide with a title, a kicker and a payoff
   line, but nothing else, so they get more room than .vrvid. */
.reveal .demovid.appvid { height: 404px; }

/* recount-explorer and genome-explorer were recorded at 1600x1000, not the
   1920x1080 every other clip uses. The base rule pins 16/9, so those two sat
   in white letterbox bars. Give them their real ratio rather than re-encoding
   the source, which would cost quality to fix a CSS problem. */
.reveal .demovid.r1610 { aspect-ratio: 16 / 10; }

/* The affordance. A paused clip on a slide is indistinguishable from a
   screenshot, so it needs to say it is a video before anyone clicks. The badge
   is drawn over the clip and removed the moment it first plays, so it is a hint
   rather than a permanent control. */
.reveal .vidwrap { position: relative; display: block; }
.reveal .vidwrap::after {
  content: "\25B6";               /* solid right-pointing triangle */
  position: absolute;
  left: 50%;
  top: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
  width: 1.9em;
  height: 1.9em;
  font-size: .8em;
  line-height: 1.95em;
  text-align: center;
  text-indent: .12em;             /* optically centres a triangle in a circle */
  color: #FFFFFF;
  background: rgba(64, 64, 65, .72);
  border-radius: 50%;
  pointer-events: none;           /* the click must reach the video underneath */
  transition: opacity .18s linear;
}
.reveal .vidwrap.played::after { opacity: 0; }

/* The act marker has to outrank whatever fills the slide behind it. Only
   GENOMES and PROMPTS remain, and GENOMES sits over the full-bleed Xenium hero,
   where without this it loses to a positioned sibling that comes later in the
   DOM. Its white pad keeps it legible; z-index keeps it visible at all. */
.reveal .act { z-index: 2; }

/* The closing thank-you photo. Deliberately NOT sized here. Quarto's
   auto-stretch (on by default, and left on) tags a lone image r-stretch and
   writes an inline height computed from whatever the slide has left, which is
   537px on this one. An inline style beats a stylesheet, so an explicit height
   rule here would be dead code that merely looked authoritative. Auto-stretch
   is doing the right thing, so let it, and set only what it does not.

   Full-bleed was the obvious alternative and is wrong here: background-size
   cover crops a 4:3 frame to its middle 75%, which lands the top of a .heroline
   scrim directly across the faces, and a thank-you slide that covers the people
   it is thanking defeats itself. */
.reveal .teamphoto {
  display: block;
  margin: .15em auto 0;
  border: 1px solid rgba(64, 64, 65, .22);
}
</style>
```

```{=html}
<script>
// Click a clip to start it, click again to pause. Deliberately NOT autoplay:
// see the .demovid comment above. The listener is delegated from the document
// rather than bound per element, because reveal clones slides for the overview
// and speaker views and handlers bound at load time do not survive the clone.
// A paused <video> paints its first frame, and the variant-reviewer recording
// opens on the app still blank, so the slide showed an empty white rectangle.
// data-poster-t names a frame worth showing instead. The first click rewinds
// to 0 so nothing is actually skipped; it is a poster, not a start point.
document.addEventListener('loadeddata', function (e) {
  var v = e.target;
  if (!v.classList || !v.classList.contains('demovid')) return;
  var t = parseFloat(v.dataset.posterT);
  if (t > 0 && !v.dataset.everPlayed) v.currentTime = t;
}, true);   // capture: loadeddata does not bubble

document.addEventListener('click', function (e) {
  var v = e.target.closest && e.target.closest('video.demovid');
  if (!v) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  var wrap = v.parentElement;
  if (v.paused) {
    if (v.dataset.posterT && !v.dataset.everPlayed) v.currentTime = 0;
    v.dataset.everPlayed = '1';
    v.play();
    if (wrap) wrap.classList.add('played');
  } else {
    v.pause();
    if (wrap) wrap.classList.remove('played');   // badge returns, so a paused
  }                                              // clip never reads as a still
});

// Leaving a slide pauses its clip, otherwise a 90-second demo keeps running
// unheard behind the next slide. It does NOT rewind: the clips are silent and
// you narrate live, so if you bump the arrow key and come back you want to
// carry on from where you were, not restart.
//
// Polled rather than guarded with `if (window.Reveal)`. This script runs inside
// slide content, which the browser executes before Quarto has initialised
// reveal, so the guard was simply false every time and the handler was never
// attached. Caught by testing the behaviour rather than by reading the code.
(function attachPauseOnLeave() {
  if (!window.Reveal || !window.Reveal.on) {
    setTimeout(attachPauseOnLeave, 120);
    return;
  }
  Reveal.on('slidechanged', function (ev) {
    if (!ev.previousSlide) return;
    ev.previousSlide.querySelectorAll('video.demovid').forEach(function (v) {
      v.pause();
      if (v.parentElement) v.parentElement.classList.remove('played');
    });
  });
})();
</script>
```

  <div><img src="assets/app-thumbnails/gene-list-builder.png"><b>gene-list-builder</b><span>A disease panel from seven sources.</span></div>

## You planned it before you paid for it

::: {.flow}
::: {}
Picked a drug

Saw the cell lines that exist.
:::

::: {}
Saw the doses

And which ones are too thin to trust.
:::

::: {}
Left with a recipe

R on one tab, Python on the other.
:::

::: {}
Downloaded nothing

Every number computed where the file lives.
:::
:::


::: {.recipe}
The app wrote this. Not an example, the export from the run you just watched.
:::

```r
library(duckdb); library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")

obs <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT * FROM read_parquet('hf://datasets/tahoebio/Tahoe-100M/metadata/obs_metadata.parquet')
  WHERE cell_name IN ('HS-578T', 'BT-474')
")
```

::: {.recipe .after}
3,094,027 cells across 1,344 samples. The other tab is the same thing in Python.
:::

::: {.payoff}
The front door for a dataset that didn't have one.
:::

## ![](assets/logos/biohttp.svg){.titlelogo} biohttp

::: {.kicker}
Every external service fails in its own way. This is the part nobody should have to write twice.
:::

::: {.bbrow}
::: {.bignums}
::: {}
7

concerns handled once
:::

::: {}
2

kinds of nothing
:::
:::

<div class="pills"><span>retry · throttle · cache · batch · timeout</span><span class="ok">CRAN</span></div>
:::

::: {.walls .g2}
::: {.w1}
The service said no

A clean empty answer. The gene is real, there is simply nothing recorded on it.
:::

::: {.w4}
The service fell over

A timeout, a 500, a rate limit. Same silence on screen, completely different problem.
:::
:::

::: {.payoff}
Telling those two apart is the whole reason an app can lean on eighteen services at once.
:::

## ![](assets/logos/bioclients.svg){.titlelogo} bioclients

::: {.kicker}
biohttp knows how to talk to a service. This one knows what each service is saying back.
:::

::: {.bbrow}
::: {.bignums}
::: {}
29

biological services
:::

::: {}
2

halves, kept apart
:::
:::

<div class="pills"><span>Ensembl · UniProt · gnomAD · ClinVar · and 25 more</span><span class="ok">CRAN</span></div>
:::

::: {.payoff}
Fetching and parsing are separate, so a stored response is enough to test a parser. No live API, no flaky test.
:::

## ![](assets/logos/biocohort.svg){.titlelogo} biocohort

::: {.kicker}
The least glamorous one, and the one my own research leans on hardest. Before an API or a figure matters, the study has to stay organised.
:::

::: {.flow}
::: {}
Subjects and samples

Who, and what came off them.
:::

::: {}
Assays

RNA, ATAC and whole genome, described in one manifest.
:::

::: {}
Corrections

A swapped label, fixed once, stays fixed.
:::

::: {}
Sample sheets

Generated from the manifest, not typed by hand.
:::
:::

<div class="pills"><span>one manifest per study · many assays · many organisms</span><span class="ok">CRAN</span></div>

::: {.payoff}
These are cheap problems early and very expensive ones later.
:::
